newsitem.title: CYPRUS: I made no promises to US, says Cyprus's Clerides.
newsitem.headline: I made no promises to US, says Cyprus's Clerides.

text.p: Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides on Tuesday dismissed suggestions he gave the United States a pledge Greek warplanes would not be deployed for the next 13 months to a new airbase under construction on the divided Mediterranean island.

"Yes, we are building an air base but we have not taken a decision yet as to whether the planes will park here or come for refuelling," Clerides told a panel of journalists in an interview aired live on television stations on Tuesday night.
"Our side has not yet taken a decision... whether they will be Greek planes, Cypriot planes, whether they will be mixed planes, stationed here or just use the base for refuelling," he said.
"I did not commit myself. I outlined our positions (to the Americans) as I did now," he said.

The eastern Mediterranean island's Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities have been divided since Turkey invaded Cyprus's northern third in the wake of a brief Greek Cypriot coup in capital Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
A Turkish Cypriot state declared in the north in 1983 is recognised only by Ankara, which has some 30,000 troops in northern Cyprus.

Decades-old efforts sprearheaded by the United Nations to reunite the island under a federal umbrella have floundered, and the dispute remains a source of tension between NATO partners Greece and Turkey.
International efforts to add impetus to the search for a solution have recently gained pace as the island gears up for entry negotiations to the European Union next year.
Under a 1993 defence pact with Greece, Cyprus is building the military air base in the coastal western town of Paphos which could accomodate Greek warplanes in the event of a renewed crisis.
Clerides said the base would be completed by the end of the year. Slight delays in the completion of construction, he said, were due to modifications on the original plans.

Tensions in the region flared last month after disclosures Cyprus had concluded a deal with Russia to purchase surface-to-air S-300 missiles, and Turkish threats of military action to prevent deployment of the system.
Clerides said the system was necessary for the security of Cyprus.
A U.S. envoy deployed to the region last month said the crisis was defused after recieving assurances from Clerides that the system would not be deployed for 16 months.

Clerides attributed the delay to technical reasons. "In spite of my efforts, and I made efforts for them to be delivered sooner, the Russians told us it was impossible to deliver them (sooner). It is a minimum period of 16 months, and not for all of the quantity, only half of the quantity (ordered)," he said.

He said some components of the system would be delivered 16 months after the agreement is ratified by the island's parliament which will release the necessary funds for a deposit on the 200 million pound ($404 million) system.
Approval of the deal there is still pending.
